views.title: Agent team · 12 markets
views.label: Synthetic business · real weather and holidays · simulated outcomes
views.blurb: A consumer brand in 12 cities and 4 product lines, about €3.3M of marketing a month across 8 paid channels plus email, SMS and organic. A team of AI agents read every source, the growth lead decided, and each decision was run forward a quarter against doing nothing.

ent.headline: Since 14 Oct, iOS checkout in Paris and Amsterdam has completed only 22% of checkouts instead of about 62%, across all four lines, costing about €1.4M of revenue a month. Engineering has to fix it, and that comes before any budget change.

findings.title: iOS checkout/payment broken in Paris and Amsterdam since 14 Oct
findings.evidence: SQL check: Paris iOS checkout-to-order 62.0% \u2192 22.0% (25,731 checkouts), Amsterdam 61.9% \u2192 22.1% (11,350). London iOS 61.8% \u2192 62.2%. Payment-problem comments: Paris 12.1% (26/214), Amsterdam 15.5% (33/213), vs about 2.5% elsewhere. Lost revenue about \u20ac976k/month in Paris and \u20ac428k in Amsterdam (AOV about \u20ac60). Amsterdam NPS fell from \u22121 to \u221217.

findings.title: Barcelona organic search fell about 38% after a site change
findings.evidence: Sessions dropped from 83.7k to 54.8k in one week (week 38) and have stayed at about 50k. Revenue is about \u20ac40k a week below before, roughly \u20ac170k a month. Website-UX comments are 16.7% (37/221) vs 3.8% elsewhere, with customers reporting Google links that error and site search not working.

findings.title: The mix model says Google brand and Meta retargeting are saturated, while TikTok, creators, affiliates and YouTube are under-funded
findings.evidence: Extra revenue per extra euro: Google brand \u20ac0.07\u20130.62 and Meta retargeting \u20ac0.13\u20130.80 in Europe and New York, vs TikTok up to \u20ac8.08, creators up to \u20ac5.88 and affiliates \u20ac6.44. Model fit is good (R\u00b2 \u2265 0.7) on 24 of 44 market-lines. The plan's gain at unchanged spend is about \u20ac135k revenue a week, of which \u20ac62.7k a week is on long-history, good-fit lines.

findings.title: Paris Home captures only 64% of its search demand
findings.evidence: Paris Home makes 14.24 orders per 1,000 category searches vs 22.11 for peers. Other Paris lines capture 89\u201392%. An extra euro returns about \u20ac2.60 (4th best of 44 market-lines), and \u20ac6.44 on affiliates. Part of the gap is the checkout fault.

findings.title: Rain raises Home and Gifts demand and lowers Fashion drops
findings.evidence: Gifts: Paris +32.8%, Milan +31.8% [28.1, 35.6], Berlin +27.2% [24.0, 30.6]. Home: Barcelona +17.7% [14.8, 20.7], London +17.1%. Fashion drops \u22124% to \u221214% in every market. Beauty's effect is under 4%, which is within model error. Based on 229\u2013434 days per market-line.

findings.title: Milan late deliveries are hurting repeat buying
findings.evidence: Late-delivery comments are 24.2% (54/223) vs 6.4% elsewhere, starting the week of 5 Oct. Repeat share is 8.1% vs 11.3% in the prior period and 11.5\u201313.3% for peers. About \u20ac77k a month at stake (estimate).

findings.title: London overspent October by 22.5%
findings.evidence: \u20ac441,179 spent against \u20ac360,000 budgeted. The current run rate is \u20ac419.7k a month. Spend is up 14.9% over the last 28 days while paid revenue rose only 3.4%.

findings.title: Mexico City launch is far behind earlier launches
findings.evidence: Revenue is \u20ac1,999 a day, 5% of the earlier launches at the same age. CPA is \u20ac36.30 vs \u20ac19\u201322 for peers. About half of search demand is captured. Brand-distrust comments are 14.5% of feedback.

benchmark_analyst.summary: iOS checkout broke on 14 Oct in Paris and Amsterdam, across all four lines. Orders per iOS checkout fell from about 62% to about 22% while Android, desktop, peers and last year all held at about 62%, losing about €1.4M of revenue a month; ads can't fix this, it is an engineering problem. Beyond that, one Berlin Gifts ad is worn out, the Mexico City launch runs at 5% of earlier launches, and Lisbon's low revenue is normal for that market.

findings.title: iOS checkout-to-order collapse since 2026-10-14
findings.evidence: iOS checkout-to-order went from 61.3% on 13 Oct to 21.5% on 14 Oct and stayed near 22%. Since 14 Oct: 25,731 iOS checkouts → 5,657 orders (22.0%) vs 61.98% in 14 Sep–11 Oct (n=36,939). Clearly significant after correcting for 36 comparisons. Peer iOS range 61.65–62.37%; last year 62.0%. Android 61.9% and desktop 61.0% unaffected. AOV €60.03. Lost revenue at the normal 62% rate: about €976k/month. Paris revenue/day €84.7k vs €107.4k last year.

findings.title: iOS checkout-to-order collapse since 2026-10-14 (same break as Paris)
findings.evidence: iOS went from 61.8% on 13 Oct to 20.8% on 14 Oct. Since 14 Oct: 11,350 checkouts → 2,504 orders (22.1%). Peer iOS range 61.65–62.57%; last year 61.4%. Android and desktop at about 62%. AOV €59.75. Lost revenue about €428k/month. This also drives MER 4.78 (peer range 5.08–6.8) and CPA €26.19 (peer range 20.53–25.21).

findings.title: Ad worn out: BER-GFT-META-PROSPECTING
findings.evidence: Last 4 weeks vs prior 4: frequency 4.09 vs 2.03, CTR 0.85% vs 1.18%, orders 316 vs 533, CPA €43.7 vs €30.8 (target €25 max), spend €13,797. About 132 fewer orders than at the old CPA. Size is approximate: about €66 AOV taken from Paris/Amsterdam Gifts, as Berlin's own AOV was not pulled.

findings.title: Launch running far below earlier launches at the same age
findings.evidence: Week 8: €1,999/day vs Miami €37,189 and São Paulo €48,796 at the same age (5% of their median). CPA €36.30 vs peer range €19.27–22.18; MER 5.6 vs 5.77–7.92. Many MEX ads spent €600–2,100 for 3–19 orders each, e.g. MEX-HOM-GOOGLE-GENERIC €2,118 / 19 orders, MEX-HOM-AFFILIATES €641 / 3 orders.

findings.title: Repeat share drop
findings.evidence: Repeat share 8.08% vs 11.66% last year, 11.34% previous period, peer range 11.46–13.27%.

findings.title: Organic share below last year
findings.evidence: Organic share 40.35% vs 46.16% last year and 43.88% previous period. Peer range 40.8–47.08%, so it is only slightly below the lowest peer.

not_problems: Lisbon's revenue/day of €34.7k is below peers but matches its own last year (€35.8k) and previous period (€36.0k). It is a smaller market, not a decline.
Android and desktop checkout gaps in Amsterdam, New York, London and Berlin are under 0.6 points and are noise.
Prospecting ads at €30–55 CPA happen in every market, so being above the €25 target is not on its own an anomaly.
Paris and Amsterdam ad CPA increases are a downstream effect of the iOS checkout break, not ad fatigue: frequency and CTR are unchanged.

demand_strategist.summary: Rain moves demand reliably for Home (+9% to +18%) and Gifts (+12% to +33%) in every market, does not move Beauty in any useful way (−0.5% to +4%), and lowers Fashion drops (−4% to −14%). That supports rain rules on 23 Home and Gifts market-lines and a "pull back" rule on Fashion drops. The largest missed demand is Paris Home (64% of potential, +€1.17M gap over 8 weeks, marginal ROAS 2.6) and Mexico City at launch (about 50% of potential), but part of the Paris gap is a checkout fault across all Paris lines (55.5% vs 61.9% for peers). That fault also cuts into Paris's weather and holiday upside.

findings.title: Paris Home under-captures search demand: likely a reach or budget gap, made worse by a checkout fault
findings.evidence: demand_potential: 14.24 orders per 1,000 category searches vs 22.11 for peers, so 64% of potential is captured. The gap is 15,868 orders, €1,173,755 over 8 weeks. Other Paris lines capture 89–92%, so the shortfall is mostly specific to Home. Marginal ROAS is 2.6 (4th best of 44 cells), with affiliates' marginal ROAS at 6.44, so this looks like a reach or budget gap. Checkout-to-order is 55.18% vs a peer median of 61.89% and 61.93% last year (all Paris lines: 55.48%), and revenue per day is €33,966 vs €38,789 last year. Part of the gap is therefore a conversion problem for the checkout specialist. Monthly figure = €1.17M ÷ 8 weeks × 4.35, and should be read as an upper bound.

findings.title: Paris revenue is down 10–14.5% year on year in every line while search is flat, which points to checkout, not demand
findings.evidence: Revenue vs search interest, last 8 weeks year on year: Gifts −14.5% vs −4.3%, Fashion drops −12.1% vs +1.3%, Home −12.0% vs −2.9%, Beauty −9.9% vs +4.9%. Checkout-to-order is 55.48% vs 61.96% last year and the previous period, outside the peer range of 61.82–62.04. Demand did not fall, so Paris capture rates and forecasted uplifts are understated until checkout is fixed.

findings.title: Mexico City launch captures about half of its search demand
findings.evidence: Captured share: Home 51%, Fashion drops 48%, Gifts 52%, Beauty 51%. Capture is 9.7–11.5 orders per 1,000 searches vs 20–22 for peers. The combined 8-week gap is €385k (€114,685 + €110,442 + €92,159 + €67,735). At 8 weeks old, revenue is €1,999/day, 5% of earlier launches at the same age (Miami €37,189, São Paulo €48,796). MER is 5.39 vs a peer median of 7.81. There is no marginal-returns data for Mexico City yet. Monthly figure is a conversion of the 8-week gap.

findings.title: Rain effect is clearly positive for Home and Gifts in all markets (weather rule candidates)
findings.evidence: n = 434 days (São Paulo 300, Miami 229–230). The 95% range excludes zero in every Home and Gifts cell. Strongest: Paris Gifts +32.8% [29.5, 36.1], Milan Gifts +31.8% [28.1, 35.6], Berlin Gifts +27.2% [24.0, 30.6], Barcelona Home +17.7% [14.8, 20.7], London Gifts +17.6% [14.3, 20.9], London Home +17.1% [14.8, 19.6], Berlin Home +16.9%, São Paulo Gifts +16.7% [11.8, 21.9]. Weakest: Miami Home +9.3% [2.4, 16.7], which is a wide range and flagged not rain-sensitive in the outlook.

findings.title: Rain lowers Fashion drops demand in every market
findings.evidence: Every 95% range is below zero: Miami −14.0% [−18.8, −8.9], Berlin −7.9% [−9.8, −5.9], London −7.2% [−9.0, −5.3], Barcelona −6.8% [−9.0, −4.5], Milan −5.8%, São Paulo −5.5% [−9.8, −1.0], Lisbon −5.0%, Amsterdam −4.8%, Paris −4.7%, New York −4.6%, Madrid −4.0% [−6.6, −1.3].

findings.title: Beauty: rain effect is none or too small to act on
findings.evidence: The range includes zero in Madrid (+2.3%), Lisbon (+2.2%), London (+1.8%), Berlin (+2.2%), Amsterdam (+2.4% [−0.0, 5.0]), São Paulo (+2.2%) and Miami (+0.2%). Barcelona (+3.3%), Paris (+2.8%), Milan (+2.7%) and New York (+4.1%) are only marginally above zero. All of these are below the demand model's 7.5% error, so no rule is warranted.

not_problems: Fashion drops falling from €189k/day in Sep to about €156k/day in Nov–Dec happened last year too: it is seasonal and gets worse on rainy days.

Amsterdam revenue is down 6.5–10.6% year on year by line (€41,692/day vs €46,139), but that is inside the peer range (€35,339–55,806) and captured share is 96–101%. This is not a demand gap; keep watching it.
Madrid Beauty (109%), Lisbon Home (114%), Berlin Home (108%) and New York Home (103%) capture above peers. They are saturated, not under-served.
Small year-on-year search moves (Beauty +1.4%, Fashion drops +0.9%, Home −0.9%, Gifts −2.8% across established markets) are noise. The revenue drop beyond that comes mainly from Paris's checkout.

customer_voice_analyst.summary: Since 2026-10-14, iOS checkout has been broken in both Paris and Amsterdam. iOS checkout-to-order fell from about 62% to 34.7%, matching a new wave of complaints about declined cards and payments failing on phones. That puts about €1.4M a month at stake, and engineering should fix it first. The other new issues are broken Google links after a Barcelona site change (organic search −€5.3k/day) and late deliveries in Milan, where repeat buying has fallen below peers.

findings.title: iOS payment/checkout failure (cards declined, payment page freezes on phone)
findings.evidence: payment_problem is 12.1% of comments (26/214) vs 2.6% elsewhere and 1.8% before; NEW, p≈0. Fashion drops 14.0% (8/57). iOS checkout-to-order 61.9%→34.8% (37,878 checkouts, 13,182 orders); Android 61.8% and desktop 61.9% unchanged. All-device conversion 49.1% vs LY 61.9% and peers 61.9–62.1%. Below 50% every day since 2026-10-14 (19 days). Lost revenue vs 62% conversion is €32.5k/day.

findings.title: iOS payment/checkout failure (same bug as Paris)
findings.evidence: payment_problem is 15.5% of comments (33/213) vs 2.3% elsewhere and 2.8% before; NEW. iOS checkout-to-order 62.0%→34.7% (16,622 checkouts, 5,774 orders); Android and desktop about 62%. Started 2026-10-14. All-device 49.1% vs LY 61.7% and peers 61.9–62.2%. NPS fell from −1 to −17. Lost about €14.3k/day.

findings.title: Broken URLs / site search after a site change: organic search traffic lost
findings.evidence: website_ux is 16.7% of comments (37/221) vs 3.8% elsewhere and 5.3% before; NEW. Customers say Google links return errors since the site changed, and site search doesn't work. Organic search sessions fell from about 83k/week to about 50–55k/week starting the week of 2026-09-21. Organic search revenue per day: €14,679 before → €9,332 after. Organic share 40.4% vs LY 46.2% and peer median 45.5%.

findings.title: Late deliveries / tracking stuck; repeat purchases falling
findings.evidence: delivery_late is 24.2% of comments (54/223) vs 6.4% elsewhere and 5.1% before; NEW. Weekly count jumped from 2–5 to 19 in the week of 2026-10-05, then 14, 11, 10 (fading but not resolved). Customers report orders a week late and promised-Friday orders arriving the next Thursday. Repeat share 8.1% vs 11.3% previous period, LY 11.7%, peers 11.5–13.3%. Revenue per day €51,169 vs €53,725 previous period (within peer range). Euro figure ≈ (53,725 − 51,169) × 30.

findings.title: New market lacks brand trust
findings.evidence: trust_brand is 14.5% of comments (34/235) vs 3.1% elsewhere; persistent (13.8% before). Customers say they don't know the brand. NPS fell from −22 to −33. 8 weeks after launch, revenue is €1,999/day, 5% of what Miami and São Paulo made at the same age.

findings.title: Lisbon Fashion drop Edition 11 (LIS-FSH-E10) sold out; demand far above capacity
findings.evidence: sold_out event on 2026-10-21. Capacity 145, but 505 units recorded so far. Daily units went from 46–59 to 26–39 after selling out. Exit comments say customers left because the item was sold out. However, Lisbon's sold_out mentions are flat (13 now vs 11 before), so this is not statistically significant.

not_problems: Returns/refunds, product quality, sizing and sold-out complaints are flat or low single digits per market (for example, sizing 8–12 per market both periods). This is noise, not a new issue. Milan and Mexico City product-quality mentions actually fell.
Milan revenue per day (€51.2k) is within the peer range (€36.7k–€63.2k). The concern there is repeat buying and NPS, not a revenue collapse.
Miami NPS improved from −25 to −5, and London is stable at −6.
Amsterdam and Paris Android and desktop conversion are normal (about 62%), so the checkout problem is iOS-only and not a demand problem.

media_budget_planner.summary: The model's channel split adds an expected €135,004 a week in revenue (about €585k a month) across the 19 largest market-lines it showed. Only €62,671 a week of that comes from long-history market-lines with good fit, and the plan moves some channels by up to +79%, past its own ±50% cap. Separately, London overspent its October budget by €81,179 (122.5%), mostly on Google brand and Meta retargeting, where an extra euro returns less than €1.

findings.title: Model fit: 24 of 44 modelled market-lines fit well (R² ≥ 0.7); 8 of those 24 have short histories; Mexico City has no model
findings.evidence: R² ≥ 0.7 (24): NY ×4 (0.764–0.96), São Paulo ×4 (0.984–0.991, 42 weeks), Miami ×4 (0.987–0.993, 32 weeks), Madrid Home 0.757 and Gifts 0.93, Lisbon Home 0.787 and Gifts 0.93, London Home 0.762 and Gifts 0.932, Berlin Fashion 0.733 and Gifts 0.924, Barcelona Gifts 0.875, Paris Gifts 0.862, Milan Gifts 0.945, Amsterdam Gifts 0.755. R² 0.5–0.7 (9). R² below 0.5 (11): Paris Beauty 0.188, Paris Fashion 0.228, London Beauty 0.243, Amsterdam Beauty 0.243, Amsterdam Home 0.325, Madrid Beauty 0.356, Lisbon Fashion 0.362, Amsterdam Fashion 0.367, Berlin Beauty 0.422, Milan Fashion 0.453, Barcelona Fashion 0.489. Gifts fits well in every market; Beauty fits worst. São Paulo and Miami show R² near 0.99 on 32–42 weeks of data with 8 channels plus search as inputs, so they are probably overfitted. No holdout or uncertainty range is available from the tool. The pooled Meta prospecting elasticity (0.9747) is nearly identical to the search elasticity (~0.97), a sign that Meta prospecting is hard to separate from search demand.

findings.title: Reallocation plan: +€135,004/week revenue across the 19 largest lines shown; €62,671/week is on reliable fits
findings.evidence: Sum of expected weekly gains for the 19 market-lines the tool returned (output was cut off after that) = €135,004/week, about €585k/month, at unchanged total spend. The other 25 lines each gain ≤ €4,927/week. By fit: R² ≥ 0.7 lines = €99,511/week, of which €36,840 is São Paulo and Miami (likely overfit), leaving €62,671/week (about €272k/month) on long-history, good-fit lines (NY Home €10,846, London Home €10,032, NY Fashion €8,846, London Gifts €8,361, Paris Gifts €7,608, Madrid Home €6,185, NY Gifts €5,567, NY Beauty €5,226). Mid-fit lines €22,704/week; poor-fit lines €12,789/week (Paris Fashion R² 0.228 €7,804, Barcelona Fashion €4,985). These are revenue figures, not gross profit: no margin data exists in the hub. The plan also breaks its stated ±50% cap, with increases of +55% to +79% on TikTok, YouTube, affiliates and creators, so capped gains will be lower.

findings.title: Saturated channels: Google brand and Meta retargeting return well under €1 per extra euro
findings.evidence: Google brand marginal ROAS 0.07–0.62 in most European and NY lines (e.g. Barcelona Gifts 0.07, Paris Gifts 0.08, Amsterdam Gifts 0.10, Lisbon Beauty 0.12). Meta retargeting 0.13–0.8 (Amsterdam Beauty 0.13, Amsterdam Fashion 0.15, London Fashion 0.29). Yet last-click first-party ROAS is 9.03 for Google brand: it collects demand that would arrive anyway. Exceptions: in São Paulo and Miami these channels still return 1.06–1.97.

findings.title: Under-funded channels: TikTok, creators, affiliates and YouTube return €3–8 per extra euro on small budgets
findings.evidence: Marginal ROAS: TikTok up to 8.08 (São Paulo Gifts), 6.09 (NY Home), 5.53 (London Home); creators 5.88 (Paris Gifts), 5.62 (NY Home); affiliates 6.44 (Paris Home). Weekly spend on each is only about €600–2,500 per line, against €3,300–8,000 on Meta prospecting.

findings.title: Platforms over-claim, most on Meta retargeting, YouTube and TikTok
findings.evidence: Last 28 days, platform ROAS vs first-party ROAS: Meta retargeting 3.43 vs 1.56 (2.2×), and the model's marginal ROAS is mostly below 1. YouTube 5.90 vs 3.02 and TikTok 5.81 vs 3.24 (about 1.8–2×), but the model still puts their marginal ROAS at 3–6, so they remain under-funded despite the inflated claims. Meta prospecting 2.45 vs 1.72.

findings.title: Lines where an extra euro earns most vs lines to fund from
findings.evidence: Blended marginal ROAS. Candidates for more budget: São Paulo Gifts 3.03, São Paulo Home 2.93, Miami Home 2.83 (all short-history fits), Paris Home 2.60 (R² 0.591), Madrid Home 2.31 (R² 0.757), NY Home 2.16 (R² 0.909), London Home 2.13 (R² 0.762). Funding sources: Amsterdam Beauty 0.82, Lisbon Beauty 0.99, Amsterdam Fashion 1.06, Barcelona Beauty 1.07, Milan Beauty 1.12, Amsterdam Gifts 1.13, Paris Beauty 1.15, Madrid Beauty 1.16. The tools give no demand-capture metric, so that part of the screen could not be applied.

not_problems: Mexico City at 27.3% projected November pacing, with October at 21.5% of budget and organic +214%: it is a new market ramping up (spend only began in September). There is not enough history to model it, so it is excluded from the 44.
November pacing of 109% for Barcelona and São Paulo is based on 1 day (3.3% of the month), which is noise. Watch Barcelona because of its October overspend.
New York organic −21.9% vs the prior 28 days is only −1.2% vs last year, so it is the usual seasonal pattern.
Monthly spend at 101–104% of budget in October for most markets is mostly October's 31 days.

briefs.message: Since 14 Oct, iOS checkout in Paris and Amsterdam has completed only 22% of checkouts instead of about 62%. This hits all four lines and costs about €1.4M of revenue a month. Engineering's fix (#1) comes before any budget change. You need to decide on #2: applying the mix model's channel split across the whole portfolio, with no channel moving more than 25%. This is the only high-risk item this week.

Please decide on #4: bring London back to its €360k budget, a 14% cut. London is projected to reach 103% of budget. Please also decide on #5 (raise Paris Home's budget by 15%) and #6 (cut Lisbon Beauty's budget by 25% to pay for it). Hold #5 until the iOS checkout fix (#1) is in. The other decisions are #8 (refresh the tired Berlin Gifts Meta prospecting ad) and #12 (A/B test trust signals on Mexico City product pages). Mexico City is projected to spend only 27.3% of its €260k budget.

You have three low-risk rain rules to approve. On rainy days they raise upper-funnel spend by 30% for Milan Gifts (#9), 25% for Berlin Gifts (#10) and 20% for Barcelona Home (#11). Barcelona is projected to reach 109.1% of its €256k budget, so watch its pacing. São Paulo is also projected at 109.1%.

Nothing needs your approval this week. Since 14 Oct, iOS checkout in Paris and Amsterdam has completed only 22% of checkouts instead of about 62%. Expect more abandoned iOS checkouts in those two cities until engineering ships the fix (#1).

Your top priority is #1, the P0 fix for iOS checkout and payment in Paris and Amsterdam. Checkout completion there has been 22% instead of about 62% since 14 Oct, costing about €1.4M a month. You also need to approve #3, a ticket to SEO to restore Barcelona's old URLs with 301 redirects, resubmit the sitemap and fix site search. The last one is #7, a ticket to logistics to fix late deliveries in Milan.

The iOS checkout problem in Paris and Amsterdam is costing about €1.4M of revenue a month. Spend is a little ahead of budget in London, New York and Lisbon (each projected at 103%) and further ahead in Barcelona and São Paulo (each projected at 109.1%). Mexico City is projected to spend only 27.3% of its budget. #4 would bring London back to its €360k budget. #5 and #6 move budget from Lisbon Beauty to Paris Home and do not need your approval.

decisions.action: P0 engineering fix for iOS checkout and payment in Paris and Amsterdam
decisions.why: On 14 Oct the iOS checkout success rate fell from 62% to 22% in both markets, across all lines. Other devices and other markets were unaffected, and payment complaints rose about 5× at the same time.
decisions.expected_impact: Brings back about €1.4M of revenue a month (Paris €976k, Amsterdam €428k).
decisions.note: Markets: Paris and Amsterdam, all lines. iOS checkout-to-order went from 62.0% to 22.0% on 2026-10-14 (Paris 5,657 orders from 25,731 checkouts; Amsterdam 2,504 from 11,350). London iOS is at 62.2%, and Android and desktop are at about 62%. Customers report cards declined and the payment page freezing on iPhone. Check the payment SDK, 3DS, PSP and Apple Pay releases from 13–14 Oct, and roll back if needed. About €1.4M of revenue a month at stake.

decisions.action: Apply the mix model's channel split across the whole portfolio, with no channel moving more than 25%

executed.detail: all: channel split applied on 44 market-lines (max ±25% per channel); model expects +€141,784 revenue a week

decisions.why: Google brand and Meta retargeting return well under €1 per extra euro, while TikTok, creators, affiliates and YouTube return €3–8. The model fits well on 24 of 44 market-lines. The 25% cap limits the risk on poorly fitting lines and keeps the plan inside its own limits (uncapped, it moves some channels by up to +79%).
decisions.expected_impact: Up to €272k a month extra revenue at unchanged spend on long-history, good-fit lines; less after the cap. This is revenue, not gross profit.
decisions.note: Portfolio-wide, so Leadership approves. Each line's total stays the same. Money moves from Google brand and Meta retargeting to TikTok, creators, affiliates and YouTube, with no channel moving more than 25%. Mexico City has no model and is excluded. Lines with R² below 0.5 (Paris Fashion and Beauty, the Amsterdam lines, most Beauty) should be watched closely.

decisions.action: Ticket to SEO: restore Barcelona's old URLs (301 redirects), resubmit the sitemap and fix site search
decisions.why: Since the week of 21 Sep, organic search sessions are down from about 83k to about 50k a week, and customers say Google links return errors.
decisions.expected_impact: Brings back about €40k of revenue a week (about €170k a month).
decisions.note: Market: Barcelona. Organic search sessions fell from 83.7k to 54.8k a week in week 38 (week of 21 Sep) and have stayed at about 50k. Organic-search revenue is down from about €103k to €65k a week. Website-UX comments are 16.7% (37/221) vs 3.8% in other markets: Google links return errors and site search is broken. Add 301 redirects from the old URLs, resubmit the sitemap and fix site search.

decisions.action: Bring London spend back to its €360k budget (−14%)
decisions.why: London overspent October by €81k and is running at €420k a month. Most of the extra went to Google brand and Meta retargeting, where an extra euro returns €0.19–0.72.
decisions.expected_impact: Saves about €60k a month with little revenue lost.
decisions.note: Market: London. The 30-day run rate of €419.7k vs a €360k budget implies −14%. Make the cuts first in Google brand and Meta retargeting.

decisions.why: Paris Home captures 64% of its potential demand vs 89–92% for other Paris lines. An extra euro returns about €2.60, and €6.44 on affiliates.
decisions.expected_impact: About +€12.5k a month of spend at roughly €2.6 return per euro: about +€32k revenue a month, more once checkout is fixed.
decisions.note: Market: Paris, line: Home. Budget goes from €83k to about €95.5k a month; put the extra mainly into affiliates and creators. Funded by the Lisbon Beauty cut below. Ideally scale once the iOS checkout fix is live.

decisions.action: Cut Lisbon Beauty's budget by 25% to fund Paris Home
decisions.why: Lisbon Beauty returns €0.99 per extra euro, one of the lowest in the portfolio, and Lisbon overspent October by 7%.
decisions.expected_impact: Frees about €12.5k a month and loses roughly €12k of revenue, against about €32k gained in Paris Home.

Android and desktop in the same cities are unchanged (Amsterdam Android 526/818 = 64%; Berlin desktop 488/730 = 67%). iOS in the other 10 markets is 65.2% (10,938/16,774). Order value is unchanged at about €61.7. At the old rates that is about 579 lost orders in Amsterdam and 782 in Berlin, roughly €84k in 19 days (about €4.4k a day). It is the same in all four sectors (after 14 Sep: bar 2/38, clinic 1/39, hair salon 6/54, shop 7/39, against 27–47 per sector before). Nothing upstream changed: click-through rate is 1.13% vs 1.11%, cost per click 0.30 EUR, engaged time about 40 s, the landing page is still /de/, and the form completion rate held. Contact speed is not the cause either: 30 of 60 DE2 leads still in 'Contacted' were reached within 2 h. 53 DE2 leads were marked Lost this period. DE2 spent 638 EUR for 5 qualified leads (about 128 EUR each), against about 15 EUR each for DE2 over its lifetime. Germany as a market fell from 52.7% to 40.4% qualified, which holds after correction. The other German ads, DE1 and DE3, are normal.

findings.title: Italy: leads have been contacted slowly since late August, and qualification fell with it
findings.evidence: In Italy, leads contacted within 2 h fell from 33–44 a week to 6–15 a week from week 35 (24–30 Aug). Average time to first contact went from about 14–22 h to about 36–45 h. No other market changed (all at 16–25 h). Italy's qualified rate was 55.3% (179/324) in weeks 30–34 and 33.7% (168/499) in weeks 35–42, which holds after correction. Since 24 Aug, Italian leads reached within 2 h qualified at 80.6% (83/103), against 25.4% (116/456) for slower ones. This is observational, but it matches the business-wide pattern: 74% of leads reached within 2 h qualify, against 23% of those reached after 24 h. Compared with the previous period alone, Italy's drop (36.9% to 30.4%) is not significant, because the damage started before that period began.

findings.title: 'Before and after' is the cheapest ad concept per qualified lead and per win, and its leads close just as well
findings.evidence: Lifetime figures excluding DE2: 'Before and after' costs 12.46 EUR per qualified lead and 51.74 EUR per win. 'Owner story' costs 19.62 and 80.98 EUR; 'Prices carousel' costs 18.95 and 70.09 EUR. The share of qualified leads that end up won is the same (Owner story 24.2% vs Before and after 24.1%; no detectable difference). So the gap comes from cheaper clicks (0.30 EUR vs about 0.48–0.55 EUR), not from worse leads. The pattern repeats in all 10 markets. This period spend was split evenly: 3,690 / 3,712 / 3,738 EUR.

findings.title: The other markets are stable
findings.evidence: Portugal's qualified rate fell from 57.6% to 45.5% (80/139 to 66/145). That is p=0.04 before correction but likely noise after correcting for 10 markets. BE, AT, IE, NL, PL and ES moved by only a few leads each. Too little data to call any of them changed. Confirming a shift of Portugal's size would take about 270 leads per period, roughly two periods of Portuguese volume.

recommendations.action: Fix the French mobile form this week. Reproduce the error on a phone at /fr/ (look for validation such as phone or postcode format, a required field, a consent checkbox or a script error), using whatever was deployed around 14–20 September as the starting point.
recommendations.why: Half of the French mobile visitors who start the form are now lost to errors. This hits both paid and search traffic, so all French spend and SEO is losing leads.
recommendations.expected_impact: About 90 extra leads per 28 days at the old 52.5% mobile completion rate. At France's current rate of about 54% qualified, that is roughly 45 more qualified leads per period at zero extra spend.
recommendations.how_to_measure: Weekly French mobile errors per form start back under about 15%, and submits per start back above 50% (it was 22.6% this period).

recommendations.action: Find out what changed for DE2 around 14 September (ad text or offer, audience, placements, or how sales tags these leads). Meanwhile, cut DE2's budget by at least half and move it to DE1 and DE3.
recommendations.why: DE2 now costs about 128 EUR per qualified lead, against about 15 EUR before. Clicks, site behaviour and contact speed are unchanged, so the leads themselves (or how they are judged) changed, and only the team can see why.
recommendations.expected_impact: Moving about 320 EUR per period to DE1 and DE3 (about 18–19 EUR per qualified lead over their lifetime) should bring roughly 15 more qualified leads than DE2 would at its current rate. Fixing the root cause would bring back about 30 qualified leads per period.
recommendations.how_to_measure: Weekly DE2 qualified share (4% now, 31% before). Germany's cost per qualified lead.

recommendations.action: Bring Italian first contact back under 2 hours: check who covers Italian leads since late August (absence, new rep, language coverage, routing rule) and fix staffing or routing.
recommendations.why: Italy's qualified rate fell from 55% to 34% exactly when fast contacts dropped from about 40 to about 8 a week. Leads reached within 2 h qualify about three times as often.
recommendations.expected_impact: If Italy returns to its pre-August 55% on about 250 leads per period, that is roughly 50 more qualified leads per period (75 this period). The link is observational, so treat this as an upper bound.
recommendations.how_to_measure: Weekly share of Italian leads contacted within 2 h (now about 10%, previously about 60%) and Italy's qualified rate.

recommendations.action: Move part of each market's 'Owner story' budget to 'Before and after', for example 30% in every market except Germany, as a reversible shift. Keep the total budget unchanged.
recommendations.why: Across all markets, 'Before and after' delivers qualified leads at 12.46 EUR against 19.62 EUR, and its leads close just as well.
recommendations.expected_impact: About 1,100 EUR per period moved from about 19.6 to about 12.5 EUR per qualified lead would bring roughly 30 more qualified leads per period, if costs hold as budget grows. Watch for rising costs or ad fatigue.
recommendations.how_to_measure: Cost per qualified lead by concept and by market, every 2 weeks. Undo the shift if the 'Before and after' cost per qualified lead rises above about 17 EUR.

experiments.hypothesis: If DE2's lead quality collapsed because of the ad set itself (audience or learning drift) rather than the creative, a fresh copy will qualify at the old rate of about 30% while the original stays at about 4%.
experiments.variant: Duplicate DE2 as a new ad with the same creative and landing page /de/, in a new ad set with the original audience settings, at half of DE2's budget. Version A is the current DE2.

views.title: B2B funnel + reviews
views.label: Real public data
views.blurb: Olist's real marketing funnel (8,000 leads, 842 deals) joined to 3,000 classified customer reviews. Figures checked against the raw files.

sources.note: Olist marketing funnel and Brazilian e-commerce datasets (Kaggle, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
Olist and alternatives for small sellers in Brazil: 6 questions x 3 runs on claude-opus-5-5 with web search

memo.headline: May produced 130 closed deals against 183 in April. The drop is real and not just because May's leads are younger: the share of leads closed within 30 days started falling in the second half of April (13.1% down to 7.6%). Lead volume and channel mix hardly changed, and in the same weeks several reps stopped appearing on won deals, so the first thing to check is sales coverage, not marketing.

data_sufficiency.explanation: Lead counts are large enough (about 1,300 a month) for solid conclusions on close rates by month, channel and landing page, and the April-vs-May drop is statistically clear (p=0.0005). But there is no spend data, so no cost per lead or cost per deal. There are no contact timestamps, so response speed can't be measured. Rep (sdr/owner), sector and lead type exist only for won deals: they can show when a rep stopped closing deals, but not how many leads each rep was given or why deals are won. The 90-day merchant value is incomplete for recent cohorts (75 of May's 130 deals have it), and one merchant (75,730 BRL, 'unknown' channel) dominates value totals. The month-to-month comparison uses a fixed 'closed within 30 days' window so April and May leads get the same time to close. Note the brief's 'previous period' (Mar 31-Apr 30, 1,362 leads) is one day off calendar April (1,352); this memo uses calendar April.

kpis.name: Leads (MQLs)
kpis.note: -3.6%. Volume is flat, so it does not explain the fall in deals.

kpis.name: Closed deals from the month's leads (to date)
kpis.note: -29%. Part of this is May's leads being younger, but see the 30-day figure below.

kpis.name: Close rate (to date)
kpis.note: Statistically significant drop (p=0.0045).

kpis.name: Deals closed within 30 days of the lead
kpis.note: Same 30-day window for both months, so this is a fair comparison: -36%, p=0.0005. By half-month: Apr 1-15 13.1%, Apr 16-30 8.8%, May 1-15 7.4%, May 16-31 6.5%.

kpis.name: Won merchants selling within 90 days
kpis.note: May's 90-day data is incomplete. The share is similar; the absolute count is down because there are fewer deals.

kpis.name: Search leads (organic + paid)
kpis.note: Steady. The search channels' 30-day closes still fell: organic 45→29, paid 36→21.

kpis.name: Social leads
kpis.note: Lower-converting channel. 30-day closes 13→4.

kpis.name: Email leads
kpis.note: Nearly doubled, but only 2 won (3 in April).

findings.title: The fall in closings started mid-April and is not explained by younger leads
findings.evidence: Closed within 30 days: Apr 1-15 86/655 (13.1%) vs Apr 16-May 31 152/2,000 (7.6%), p<0.001. May vs April: 91/1,303 vs 147/1,352, p=0.0005. Every May lead has had at least 5 months to close by the November 2018 data end, and the 30-day window is fully observed for both months.

findings.title: Channel mix does not explain it: close rates fell inside each main channel
findings.evidence: Applying April's 30-day close rate per channel to May's lead mix predicts about 144 deals, close to April's actual 147. May actually got 91. Within-channel 30-day closes, April→May: organic 45/349→29/344, paid search 36/272→21/266, social 13/325→4/269, direct 11/75→5/78. 'Unknown' held best (29/166→24/154).

findings.title: Several reps stop appearing on won deals in late April, the same time the close rate fell
findings.evidence: Qualifying reps 068066e2 (81 wins all-time, last won lead Apr 20) and a8387c01 (59 wins, last won lead Apr 25) together qualified 40 of April's 183 wins and 0 of May's. Closing rep 9e4d1098 closed 18 April-lead deals and 0 May-lead deals (last lead Apr 25). Rep d3d1e91a dropped from 22 to 6 (last lead May 16). Limitation: rep fields exist only for won deals. We can't see how many leads these reps were given, so this is a strong hint about sales capacity, not proof.

findings.title: Search brings deals and merchants who sell. Social and email convert far worse
findings.evidence: Close rate for leads since Jan 2018: paid search 175/1,182 (14.8%) vs social 66/1,051 (6.3%), p<0.001, and vs email 14/347 (4.0%), p<0.001. Organic 255/1,736 (14.7%); 'unknown' 168/813 (20.7%). 90-day merchant sales per lead: paid search about 61 BRL, organic about 51, social about 12, email about 18. 'Unknown' is about 155, but one merchant at 75,730 BRL makes up 59% of that channel's all-time value. Won paid-search merchants sell within 90 days more often than organic ones: 74/135 (55%) vs 80/200 (40%), p=0.008. Merchant mix or onboarding may contribute. Without spend we can't say whether social or email are worth their cost.

findings.title: For search leads, landing page 22c29808 closes far better than e492ee and f017be
findings.evidence: Search-lead close rate since 2018: 22c29808 125/521 (24.0%) vs f017be 16/155 (10.3%), p=0.0002, and vs e492ee 7/108 (6.5%), p<0.001. In May, f017be and e492ee still received 36 and 40 leads (all channels). This is observational: the pages may serve different keywords or audiences, so it needs a controlled test before a full switch. The two social pages are no different on 30-day closes (58326e 15/464 vs 88740e 10/285, both about 3%).

findings.title: Merchants from search do not create unhappy customers. Customer reviews are better than the baseline
findings.evidence: Negative review share: organic-acquired merchants 97/446 (21.7%) and paid-search 115/469 (24.5%) vs merchants who joined outside the funnel 375/1,236 (30.3%), p=0.0005 and p=0.018. 'Other' channel is worse at 22/46 (47.8%, p=0.012), but those reviews come from only about 4 won merchants, so treat it as low confidence. The top complaint themes overall are not_delivered (12.7% of reviews) and wrong_or_missing_item (8.9%).

recommendations.action: This week, find out whether reps 068066e2, a8387c01, 9e4d1098 (and d3d1e91a) left, moved or lost their lead queue after mid-April. Reassign their open MQLs and rebalance the queue so every new lead is picked up.
recommendations.why: The 30-day close rate fell from 13.1% to 7.6% at the same time these reps stopped appearing on wins. Lead volume and channel mix didn't change.
recommendations.expected_impact: If 30-day close returns to the early-April 13.1% on about 1,300 leads a month, that is about 70 more deals a month than at 7.6%. Even half the gap is about 35.
recommendations.how_to_measure: Weekly 30-day close rate per weekly lead cohort, tracked against the 13.1% early-April benchmark.

recommendations.action: Re-contact the unclosed late-April and May MQL backlog (about 1,790 leads: 1,173 from May plus 616 from Apr 16-30). Start with search, 'unknown' and referral leads. Do it as the controlled re-contact test below.
recommendations.why: Those cohorts were probably under-worked during the coverage gap. Search and 'unknown' leads close at 15-21% when worked normally.
recommendations.expected_impact: Recovers part of the roughly 56 deals May fell short of what April's channel rates predict (about 144 expected vs 91 actual within 30 days).
recommendations.how_to_measure: Won within 30 days of re-contact, re-contacted half vs held-out half (see experiment).

recommendations.action: While capacity is short, order the SDR queue by channel: paid/organic search, 'unknown', referral and direct first; social, email, display and other last.
recommendations.why: Close rates since 2018: search about 14.8%, 'unknown' 20.7% vs social 6.3% and email 4.0%. Paid-search merchants also sell more often within 90 days (55%).
recommendations.expected_impact: Each SDR hour spent on search leads produces about 2-3x the deals of an hour on social, and 3-4x email.
recommendations.how_to_measure: Deals per SDR per week, and 30-day close rate by channel.

recommendations.action: Send paid-search traffic currently landing on f017be / e492ee to landing page 22c29808, as a split test first (separate ads or ad groups per page).
recommendations.why: Search leads on 22c29808 close at 24.0% vs 10.3% (f017be) and 6.5% (e492ee). This is observational, so confirm before a full switch.
recommendations.expected_impact: If even half the gap holds, the 76 May leads on those two pages would bring about 5-7 more deals a month.
recommendations.how_to_measure: Leads per click and 30-day close rate per page in the test.

recommendations.action: Check list quality and targeting on the email channel, which nearly doubled to 94 leads but closed 2. Hold social and email volume flat until spend figures are available.
recommendations.why: Email closes at 4.0% and social at 6.3% vs about 15% for search. More of these leads uses up SDR time when capacity is already short.
recommendations.expected_impact: Frees SDR time for higher-converting leads. Cost savings depend on spend we can't see.
recommendations.how_to_measure: Email/social share of SDR-touched leads and their close rate; cost per deal once spend is shared.

experiments.hypothesis: Unclosed late-April and May leads were under-worked during the rep gap. A structured re-contact cadence will lift their 30-day close rate. Sized on the 7.6% vs 13.1% gap between the later and early-April cohorts.
experiments.variant: B: a randomly chosen half of the unclosed Apr 16-May 31 backlog gets a fresh SDR call-plus-email cadence. A: the other half stays in the normal queue.
experiments.metric: Deals closed within 30 days of assignment

experiments.hypothesis: Paid-search leads that land on 22c29808 close at a higher rate than those landing on f017be (observed 24.0% vs 10.3%).
experiments.variant: B: paid-search ads point to landing 22c29808. A: matching ads point to f017be. Same keywords and budget split 50/50.
experiments.metric: Close rate of paid-search leads within 30 days (also leads per click)

questions_for_owner: Did reps 068066e2, a8387c01 and 9e4d1098 leave or change role around Apr 20-25? Where did their leads go? Was d3d1e91a off after mid-May?
Can you share how many leads each SDR was assigned (not just won), and the contact timestamps? Then we can measure response speed and coverage directly.
What do social, email and paid search cost per month? Without spend we can't judge whether social (6.3% close) and email (4.0%) are worth funding.
What keywords or audiences feed landing pages f017be and e492ee vs 22c29808? Can paid-search ad groups be re-pointed for a test?
What is behind the 'unknown' utm_source? It closes best (20.7%), and if it is a partner or outbound source it may be worth growing.
